Task-focused care done quickly describes functional nursing, the model the unit is leaving. Fewer RNs and lower costs is backward: primary nursing needs more RNs and costs more. Assistive personnel planning care is outside their role; in primary nursing, the primary nurse develops the plan.

Takeaway: Primary nursing trades a higher cost for continuity, accountability, and clients who know their nurse.

questions.stem: A nurse is learning about case management. Which of the following statements about case management are accurate?
options: “A case manager leads an interprofessional team that coordinates the client's care.”
“The case manager may be a nurse, a social worker, or another member of the health care team.”
“Case management is most needed when a client has many care needs and several providers.”
“The case manager gives all of the client's direct care during each shift.”
“Case management can cover one hospital stay or follow the client into the community.”
“Only clients who have private insurance can receive case management.”
questions.rationale:
Case management is a collaborative process in which an interprofessional team, led by a case manager, coordinates care. The case manager may be a nurse, a social worker, or another team member. It's essential when a client has multiple care needs requiring multiple providers, and it may be limited to one hospitalization or follow the client across community settings.

The case manager coordinates care rather than giving all direct care each shift, which describes total patient care. Case management isn't limited to private insurance: hospitals, Medicare and Medicaid programs, and community agencies all use it.

Takeaway: The case manager is the coordinator for complex needs across providers and settings.

questions.stem: A nurse in a walk-in clinic is caring for a 29-year-old client who has asthma. The client lost their job and health insurance last month and is running out of their inhaler. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
options: Refer the client to a social worker to check eligibility for Medicaid or marketplace coverage
Tell the client that the clinic can't provide care without insurance
Give the client information about a community health center with sliding-scale fees
Advise the client to use the emergency department for routine refills, because it can't refuse care
Help the client look into a low-cost generic or a manufacturer's assistance program for the inhaler
questions.rationale:
A nurse can help a client without insurance by referring to a social worker or case manager (the client may qualify for Medicaid or for marketplace coverage under the Affordable Care Act), pointing the client to community health centers with sliding-scale fees and free clinics, and finding lower-cost medications through generics or manufacturer assistance programs.

Refusing care without insurance abandons the client and ignores these resources. Using the emergency department for routine refills is costly and inappropriate: emergency departments must screen and stabilize anyone with an emergency, but they aren't a source of routine care.

Takeaway: No insurance doesn't mean no care: refer, connect the client to sliding-scale clinics, and find affordable medications.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a class about social determinants of health. Which of the following definitions should the nurse use?
options: The genetic traits and family history that raise a person's risk of disease
The personal habits, such as smoking and diet, that a person chooses
The services that a person's health insurance plan will pay for
The conditions where people are born, live, learn, work, play, and age that affect their health
questions.rationale:
The conditions where people are born, live, learn, work, play, and age is correct. Social determinants of health (SDOH) are the social and environmental conditions that affect health, functioning, and quality-of-life outcomes and risks.

Genetic traits and family history are biological risk factors that can't be changed, not SDOH. Personal habits like smoking and diet are individual behaviors, though SDOH strongly shape them. Insurance benefits are one part of health care access, too narrow to define SDOH.

Takeaway: SDOH are about the conditions around a person, not their genes or their individual choices.

questions.stem: A nurse is completing a social determinants of health screening with a client. Which of the following findings are social determinants of health?
options: Lives in an apartment with mold and pests
Has a family history of breast cancer
Didn't finish high school
Is 78 years old
Smokes a pack of cigarettes a day
questions.rationale:
Housing with mold and pests (neighborhood and built environment) and not finishing high school (education access and quality) are social determinants of health: conditions in the places where people live, learn, and work.

Family history and age are biological factors that can't be changed, so they aren't SDOH. Smoking is an individual health behavior. SDOH can shape it, through stress or tobacco marketing in a neighborhood, for example, but the behavior itself isn't an SDOH.

Takeaway: Age, genes, and personal habits aren't SDOH; housing, education, income, and community are.

questions.stem: A client tells the nurse, “The last time I went to that clinic, the staff made fun of my accent, so I haven't gone back.” Which of the following barriers to care does this statement describe?
options: A geographic barrier
Discrimination and mistrust of the health care system
A financial barrier
Low health literacy
questions.rationale:
Discrimination and mistrust is correct. Being treated with disrespect because of an accent is discrimination, and it leads to mistrust and avoiding care: a barrier that limits access even when care is nearby and affordable.

A geographic barrier is distance, or living where few providers practice. A financial barrier is cost or a lack of insurance. Low health literacy is trouble finding, understanding, and using health information. None of these is what the client describes.

Takeaway: Access barriers aren't only money and miles: discrimination and mistrust keep people away too.

questions.stem: A nurse is helping an urban clinic reduce barriers to care for its clients. Which of the following strategies address barriers to access?
options: Offering visits by video or phone
Using a qualified medical interpreter service
Providing bus passes or a ride service for appointments
Requiring payment in full before each visit
Writing teaching materials in plain language at a 5th- to 6th-grade reading level
Charging fees on a sliding scale based on income
questions.rationale:
Each correct strategy removes a barrier: video or phone visits (distance and transportation), qualified interpreters (language), bus passes or rides (transportation), plain-language materials at a 5th- to 6th-grade level (health literacy), and sliding-scale fees (cost).

Requiring payment in full before each visit adds a financial barrier, and keeps clients with low incomes away.

Takeaway: Match each strategy to a barrier: distance, transportation, language, literacy, or cost.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how Healthy People 2030 groups the social determinants of health. Complete the sentence.
questions.text: The five domains are economic stability, {{0}}, health care access and quality, {{1}}, and social and community context.
questions.rationale:
The five domains are economic stability, education access and quality, health care access and quality, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context.

Genetics and family history are biological factors, and personal health behaviors are individual choices; neither is a domain of the social determinants. Insurance plan benefits fall within health care access, not a separate domain.

Takeaway: The five SDOH domains: economic stability, education, health care access, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing a client who has been living in a homeless shelter for discharge after surgery. Which of the following actions best addresses a social determinant of health?
options: Reminding the client that smoking slows wound healing
Teaching the client to take medications at the same time each day
Referring the client to a social worker for help finding stable housing
Encouraging the client to walk for 30 minutes each day
questions.rationale:
Referring the client to a social worker for stable housing is correct. Housing is a social determinant of health, and a shelter makes wound care, rest, and storing medications hard. Addressing it gives the rest of the discharge teaching a chance to work.

Smoking, medication timing, and walking are individual health behaviors. Teaching about them is good care, but it doesn't address the conditions the client lives in.

Takeaway: To address an SDOH, change the client's conditions (housing, food, income, transportation), not only their behavior.

questions.stem: A nurse who worked for 5 years at one hospital starts a job at another hospital whose procedures are different. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?
options: Learn and follow the new hospital's policies and procedures
Keep using the old hospital's procedures, since they worked well
Follow whichever procedure takes less time for each task
Ask each client which procedure they would prefer
questions.rationale:
Learn and follow the new hospital's policies and procedures is correct. Each agency has its own policies and procedures, and nurses are accountable for knowing and following the requirements of the agency where they practice. If the nurse believes a procedure should change, the nurse can propose it through the agency's process.

Using the old hospital's procedures, choosing the fastest method, and letting clients choose the procedure all step outside the agency's standards, which puts clients and the nurse at risk.

Takeaway: Accountability means practicing by your current agency's policies and procedures.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how health care systems relate to other nursing concepts. For each nursing action, specify the concept it best reflects.
rows: Gives a structured handoff when the client transfers to a rehabilitation center
Applies the same criteria to every client when deciding who gets a scarce resource
Follows the agency's procedure for central line care and answers for the care given
Speaks up when a client is about to be discharged without a safe way to get home
questions.rationale:
Communication: a structured handoff keeps care continuous across settings. Ethics: applying the same criteria to everyone is justice in allocating scarce resources. Accountability: following agency policy and answering for the care given. Advocacy: speaking up so the client can overcome a barrier and leave safely.

Takeaway: Health care systems connect to accountability (policies), advocacy (barriers), communication (handoffs), collaboration (teams), and ethics (justice).

questions.stem: A hospital is considering changing a medical unit from team nursing to total patient care. Which of the following effects should the nurse manager expect?
options: More RNs will be needed, which will raise staffing costs
Clients' care will become more fragmented and task-focused
Assistive personnel will take on more of each client's care
Staffing costs will fall, because the unit will need fewer staff
questions.rationale:
More RNs, and higher staffing costs is correct. In total patient care, one RN gives all of the care for assigned clients during the shift. That gives holistic care and clear accountability, but it takes many RNs, so it's expensive. A care delivery model affects the budget as well as client outcomes and safety.

Fragmented, task-focused care describes functional nursing. Assistive personnel taking on more care describes team and functional nursing, which use them for tasks; total patient care relies on RNs. Costs falling is backward, because RNs replace less costly team members.

Takeaway: Every care delivery model has a trade-off; total patient care buys holistic care at the cost of more RNs.

questions.stem: A nurse is floated to an unfamiliar unit that uses team nursing. Which of the following actions should the nurse take first?
options: Ask the team leader to clarify the nurse's assignment and which tasks are delegated to whom
Begin giving medications to the clients who seem the sickest
Ask the assistive personnel which tasks they would like to do
Use the routines from the nurse's home unit until someone corrects them
questions.rationale:
Clarifying the assignment with the team leader is correct. In team nursing, the RN team leader is accountable for the team's clients and assigns tasks. A floating nurse must know their role, the unit's expectations, and who is doing what before acting, to keep care safe.

Starting medications on the sickest-looking clients skips getting a report and an assignment. Letting assistive personnel pick tasks isn't how delegation works; the RN assigns tasks based on ability. Using home-unit routines ignores this unit's policies.

Takeaway: On a new unit, know your role and the model first: clarify the assignment before you act.

questions.stem: A client's insurance plan denies coverage for home health visits that the provider ordered after the client's hospital stay. Which of the following actions by the nurse best reflects advocacy?
options: Telling the client to pay for the visits out of pocket
Canceling the home health referral, since it won't be covered
Contacting the case manager to help the client appeal or find another way to get the service
Advising the client to come back to the emergency department if problems start
questions.rationale:
Working with the case manager to appeal or find another option is correct. Advocacy means helping clients overcome barriers to the care they need, and case managers know payer rules, appeals, and community resources.

Paying out of pocket may not be possible, and it skips the client's other options. Canceling the referral leaves the client without needed care. Using the emergency department waits for a problem instead of preventing it, and it's costly.

Takeaway: When the system blocks needed care, the nurse advocates, often through the case manager.

questions.stem: A client who had a stroke is going home next week. Which of the following actions best reflects interprofessional collaboration in planning the client's move home?
options: The nurse writes the discharge plan alone and gives it to the client on the day of discharge.
The nurse, therapists, social worker, client, and family meet to plan the client's care at home.
Each discipline gives the client separate instructions without comparing them.
The provider decides on all services, and the nurse carries out the orders.
questions.rationale:
The team meeting with the client and family is correct. Interprofessional collaboration brings each discipline's expertise together, with the client and family, so the plan is coordinated and realistic.

A plan written alone leaves out the other disciplines and the family. Separate instructions create fragmented and sometimes conflicting care. The provider deciding everything leaves out the team's and the client's input.

Takeaway: Collaboration means everyone, including the client and family, plans together.

questions.stem: A nurse manager must reduce the unit's supply costs by 10%. Which of the following actions best balances cost with safe care?
options: Reusing single-use supplies after cleaning them
Delaying dressing changes to make supplies last longer
Using the least expensive dressing for every wound, whatever the type
Opening supplies only when they're needed, to reduce waste
questions.rationale:
Opening supplies only when they're needed is correct. Nurses help allocate limited resources by using supplies cost-consciously and avoiding waste, without compromising care.

Reusing single-use items risks infection and violates infection-control standards. Delaying dressing changes risks infection and poor healing. The cheapest dressing for every wound ignores what each wound needs, and can cost more if wounds heal poorly.

Takeaway: Save resources by cutting waste, never by cutting safe care.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentences about allocating limited health care resources.
questions.text: Distributing scarce resources fairly reflects the ethical principle of {{0}}. During a disaster, the goal of allocation becomes {{1}}.

options: autonomy
veracity
distributive justice
fidelity
treating clients in the order they arrive
doing the greatest good for the greatest number of people
treating clients who can pay first
saving every client, whatever it costs

questions.rationale:
Distributive justice is the fair, equitable distribution of resources. When demand far exceeds supply, as in a disaster, the goal shifts to doing the greatest good for the greatest number.

Autonomy is the client's right to decide, veracity is truthfulness, and fidelity is keeping promises. First come, first served and ability to pay aren't fair or effective ways to allocate, and saving everyone at any cost isn't possible when resources run out.

Takeaway: Scarce resources call for justice; disasters call for the greatest good for the greatest number.

questions.stem: A nurse is triaging victims of a bus crash using a mass-casualty triage system. For each victim, specify the triage category.
rows: Walking around the scene with abrasions and a sprained wrist
Respiratory rate 34/min, confused, capillary refill 4 seconds
Not breathing, even after the airway is opened
Closed fracture of the lower leg; can't walk; alert, with a normal respiratory rate and pulse
questions.rationale:
In a mass-casualty event, the goal is the greatest good for the greatest number. Green (minor) is the walking wounded, like the victim with abrasions and a sprain. Red (immediate) is a life-threatening problem that can be treated now: a respiratory rate over 30/min, confusion, and a capillary refill over 2 seconds signal respiratory failure and shock. Black (expectant) is a victim who isn't breathing after the airway is opened. Yellow (delayed) is a serious but stable injury, like a closed leg fracture with normal breathing, pulse, and mental status.

Takeaway: Triage puts limited resources where they'll save the most lives: red first, then yellow, then green.

questions.stem: A medical unit is two nurses short for the night shift, and no replacements are available. Which of the following actions should the staff nurse take?
options: Refuse the assignment and leave at the end of the previous shift
Ask assistive personnel to give the oral medications
Skip documentation for the shift to save time
Report the unsafe staffing through the chain of command and help the charge nurse prioritize care
questions.rationale:
Reporting through the chain of command and helping prioritize is correct. When resources are short, the nurse advocates for safe staffing through the proper channels, and helps prioritize care (airway, breathing, circulation; unstable before stable) with what's available.

Leaving without a replacement can be client abandonment. Assistive personnel giving medications is outside their scope. Skipping documentation violates standards and puts clients and the nurse at legal risk.

Takeaway: When short-staffed, speak up through the chain of command, then prioritize; never abandon clients or delegate outside someone's scope.

questions.stem: A medical unit has one telemetry bed available, and four clients are being considered for it. Which client should the nurse recommend for the bed?
options: A client who has long-standing atrial fibrillation with a heart rate controlled at 70 to 80/min for 2 days
A client on day 3 after a hip replacement whose vital signs have been stable
A client who has cellulitis of the leg and a normal ECG
A client admitted with chest pain who has new ST-segment changes on the ECG
questions.rationale:
The client with chest pain and new ST changes is correct. When resources are limited, the nurse helps decide who needs them most, putting unstable before stable and acute before chronic. New ST changes with chest pain suggest acute cardiac ischemia, which needs continuous monitoring.

Controlled atrial fibrillation is chronic and stable. Stable vital signs after a hip replacement and cellulitis with a normal ECG don't call for cardiac monitoring.

Takeaway: Give a scarce resource to the client who is unstable and most likely to benefit.

questions.stem: During a shortage of influenza vaccine, a clinic must decide who receives its limited supply first. Which of the following clients should the nurse identify as priorities?
options: A 72-year-old client who has heart failure
A healthy 24-year-old college student
A client who is 28 weeks pregnant
A resident of a long-term care facility
A healthy 50-year-old office worker
A healthy 16-year-old athlete
questions.rationale:
When a resource is scarce, it goes first to the people at greatest risk of serious harm, which does the greatest good and reflects justice. Older adults with chronic illness, pregnant clients, and long-term care residents are at high risk of severe influenza and its complications.

The healthy 24-year-old, 50-year-old, and 16-year-old are at lower risk, so they can wait until more vaccine is available.

Takeaway: In a shortage, allocate by risk and benefit, using the same criteria for everyone.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings from the community assessment that are barriers limiting residents' access to health care.
questions.passage:
Most adults work [[hourly jobs with no paid time off]].
The only clinic is [[open Monday to Friday, 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.]]
The [[nearest hospital is 18 miles away]].
The bus runs [[every 90 minutes, with no service on Sundays]].
[[21% of adults have no health insurance]].
An [[active faith community runs a Saturday food pantry]].
The [[public library offers free internet]].
A [[new walking trail runs along the river]].
questions.rationale:
The barriers are hourly jobs with no paid time off (a visit means lost pay), a clinic open only during weekday working hours, a hospital 18 miles away, infrequent buses with no Sunday service (and many households have no car), and a high rate of uninsured adults. Each one limits whether residents can get care, whatever their health needs.

The food pantry, free internet at the library, and the walking trail are community strengths, resources a program can build on, not barriers.

Takeaway: Access barriers include cost, distance, transportation, and service hours that don't fit people's lives; note the community's strengths too.

questions.stem: The coalition lists programs that could address the health data. For each program, specify the level of prevention it represents.
rows: Scheduling mammograms for women ages 50 to 74
Teaching children who have asthma, and their families, to use an asthma action plan
Offering childhood vaccines on evenings and Saturdays
Running a support group for women being treated for breast cancer
Teaching middle-school students how to avoid starting to smoke
questions.rationale:
Primary prevention keeps disease from developing: childhood vaccines and smoking-prevention teaching.

Secondary prevention finds disease early: scheduling screening mammograms, which could lower the high rate of breast cancers found at a late stage.

Tertiary prevention limits complications and supports people with an established disease: asthma action plans for children who have asthma, which can cut emergency visits, and a support group for women being treated for breast cancer.

Takeaway: Match the program to the disease's stage: none yet (primary), hidden or early (secondary), established (tertiary).

questions.stem: The nurse is analyzing why so few children in the neighborhood are up to date on their vaccines. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The finding that best explains the low childhood vaccination rate is that {{0}}, so the nurse's first step should be to {{1}}.

options: the nearest hospital is 18 miles away
one in three households has an income below the poverty line
the only clinic is open on weekdays during the hours parents work hourly jobs
21% of adults have no health insurance
tell parents that vaccines are required for school
offer vaccine clinics on evenings and weekends in the neighborhood
build a new hospital closer to the neighborhood
mail parents written vaccine schedules

questions.rationale:
The best explanation is that the only clinic is open during the hours parents work hourly jobs with no paid time off: getting a child vaccinated means losing pay. So the first step is to offer vaccine clinics on evenings and weekends in the neighborhood, which removes that barrier directly.

The hospital's distance doesn't matter for vaccines, which are given in clinics. Poverty and uninsured adults are real problems, but children in low-income families can usually get vaccines through Medicaid, CHIP, or free public programs, so cost isn't the main barrier here. Telling parents vaccines are required and mailing schedules don't fix the hours problem, and a new hospital is far beyond the grant.

Takeaway: Find the barrier that best explains the data, then remove that barrier.

questions.stem: The grant can fund only one of the coalition's proposals. Which proposal should the nurse recommend?
options: A: Discounted memberships at a private gym 12 miles away
B: Billboards about healthy eating along the highway
C: A mobile health van offering childhood vaccines and mammogram referrals on evenings and Saturdays
D: A new advanced imaging machine for the hospital 18 miles away
questions.rationale:
The mobile health van is correct. It targets the neighborhood's biggest gaps (low vaccination and mammogram rates, late-stage breast cancers), removes its main barriers (work hours, distance, transportation), and produces measurable results within a year. That's a fair allocation of limited resources that does the most good for the most people.

Gym memberships 12 miles away help mostly residents who already have cars and money. Billboards don't remove any barrier and are hard to measure. An imaging machine at a distant hospital uses the whole grant on a service residents can't easily reach, and doesn't address the gaps in the data.

Takeaway: When resources are limited, choose the option that meets the greatest need, removes real barriers, and reaches the most people.

questions.stem: One year later, the nurse compares the neighborhood's data with the original assessment. For each finding, specify whether it shows improvement, no change, or a decline.
rows: Children up to date on vaccines by age 2: 68% → 86%
Women ages 50 to 74 with a recent mammogram: 49% → 50%
Emergency department visits for asthma, per 1,000 children: 24 → 31
Adults with no health insurance: 21% → 14%
questions.rationale:
Vaccination rates rose from 68% to 86%, and uninsured adults fell from 21% to 14%: both improved. Mammogram rates barely moved (49% to 50%), so referrals alone didn't close that gap, and the nurse should look at what still stands in the way, such as getting to the imaging site. Asthma emergency visits rose from 24 to 31 per 1,000 children, a decline in health that needs attention in the next plan.

Takeaway: Evaluate against the baseline data: keep what worked, and revise the plan where results didn't change or got worse.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is describing how evidence-based practice began in nursing. Which of the following contributions did Florence Nightingale make?
options: She defined evidence-based medicine as the use of current best evidence with clinical expertise.
She founded a library of systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials.
She named evidence-based practice one of six core competencies for nurses.
She collected and analyzed death rates, showing that better sanitation reduced deaths.
questions.rationale:
She collected and analyzed death rates is correct. During the Crimean War in the 1850s, Nightingale gathered and analyzed mortality data and showed that sanitation saved lives. Using data to change practice makes her the first nurse researcher.

Defining evidence-based medicine came in the 1990s, from Sackett and colleagues. A library of systematic reviews describes the Cochrane Collaboration, inspired by Archie Cochrane. Six core competencies describes QSEN, in the 2000s.

Takeaway: Evidence-based practice in nursing goes back to Nightingale, who used data to improve care.

questions.stem: A nurse learns that research published several years ago found a better way to prevent a common complication, but most units still use the older method. Which of the following terms describes this situation?
options: The theory-practice gap
Informed consent
Benchmarking
Peer review
questions.rationale:
The theory-practice gap is correct. It's the delay between what research shows and what's actually done in practice. Evidence-based practice aims to close it by moving the best evidence into everyday care.

Informed consent is a research participant's voluntary agreement to take part. Benchmarking compares an organization's outcomes with those of leaders in high-quality care, a quality improvement tool. Peer review is experts evaluating an article before it's published.

Takeaway: When practice lags behind the evidence, that's the theory-practice gap, and EBP is the bridge.

questions.stem: A nurse manager is listening to staff discuss how they decide on care. Which of the following statements reflect evidence-based practice rather than tradition?
options: “We've always done it this way, and it seems to work fine.”
“We changed our routine after reviewing current studies and asking clients what they prefer.”
“The charge nurse prefers this method, so that's what we use.”
“I combine the best evidence with my experience and what the client wants.”
“Let's check what the latest guideline recommends for this situation.”
questions.rationale:
Evidence-based practice combines the best current evidence, the nurse's clinical expertise, and the client's preferences. Changing a routine after reviewing studies and asking clients, combining evidence, experience, and the client's wishes, and checking the latest guideline all reflect it.

“We've always done it this way” and “the charge nurse prefers it” are tradition and authority, not evidence. Practices based on tradition can continue long after research shows a better way.

Takeaway: EBP asks “What does the evidence show, and what does this client want?” instead of “How have we always done it?”

questions.stem: A surgical unit still keeps all clients on bed rest for 24 hours after abdominal surgery “because we always have,” although current evidence supports getting clients up and walking early. Which of the following concerns is the most important for the nurse to raise?
options: Nurses on the unit may find the routine less convenient
Clients may develop complications, such as blood clots and pneumonia, that early walking helps prevent
The unit may spend more on bed linens
Clients may ask why other hospitals do things differently
questions.rationale:
Preventable complications is correct. The main risk of practicing by tradition instead of evidence is that clients get less effective or even harmful care. Immobility raises the risk of blood clots, pneumonia, and other complications that early walking helps prevent.

Convenience for nurses, linen costs, and clients' questions are minor next to harm to clients, and none of them is the reason EBP matters.

Takeaway: Tradition's biggest risk is client harm: outdated care can cause complications that evidence-based care prevents.

questions.stem: Which of the following actions by a staff nurse best helps close the theory-practice gap on the nurse's unit?
options: Continuing current routines until a supervisor brings up new research
Changing the unit's shared procedure for the nurse's own clients without telling anyone
Sharing a current guideline at a staff meeting and asking the practice council to review the procedure
Leaving research to nurse researchers, since staff nurses don't use it
questions.rationale:
Sharing the guideline and asking the practice council to review the procedure is correct. Staff nurses help close the gap between research and practice by bringing current evidence forward and using the facility's process to update practice.

Waiting for a supervisor leaves the gap open. Changing a shared procedure on one's own bypasses policy, which nurses must follow as written until it's changed. Leaving research to researchers is a misperception: every nurse uses evidence, and EBP is part of a staff nurse's accountability.

Takeaway: Every nurse can narrow the theory-practice gap by bringing evidence forward through the proper channels.

questions.stem: Complete the following sentence about how evidence-based practice became an expectation for every nurse.
questions.text: In the early 2000s, reports from the {{0}} named evidence-based practice a core competency for all health professionals, and {{1}} listed it as one of six competencies for nurses.

options: American Hospital Association
Food and Drug Administration
Institute of Medicine (IOM)
World Health Organization
Healthy People
QSEN (Quality and Safety Education for Nurses)
OSHA
Medicare

questions.rationale:
The Institute of Medicine (IOM), in reports such as Crossing the Quality Chasm and Health Professions Education, named EBP a core competency for all health professionals. QSEN then listed EBP as one of six competencies that nursing programs teach, along with patient-centered care, teamwork and collaboration, quality improvement, safety, and informatics.

The American Hospital Association, the FDA, and the WHO didn't set these competencies. Healthy People sets national health objectives, OSHA covers workplace safety, and Medicare is an insurance program.

Takeaway: EBP went from Nightingale's data to a core competency (IOM, QSEN) expected of every nurse.

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining evidence-based practice to a nursing student. Which of the following definitions is the most complete?
options: Combining the best current research with the nurse's clinical expertise and the client's preferences
Following the results of the most recent research study, whatever the client prefers
Combining research evidence with the nurse's clinical expertise
Providing care the way experienced nurses on the unit have always provided it
questions.rationale:
Research, clinical expertise, and client preferences is correct. EBP has three components: the best current research evidence, the nurse's clinical expertise, and the client's preferences, which reflect their needs, interests, and choices.

Following the latest study whatever the client prefers leaves out expertise and the client. Research plus expertise leaves out the client's preferences, a common incomplete definition. The way experienced nurses always have is tradition.

Takeaway: If a definition of EBP leaves out the client's preferences, it's incomplete.

questions.stem: Strong evidence supports walking soon after surgery. A client who had surgery yesterday declines to walk this afternoon, saying, “I'm too exhausted. Maybe this evening.” Which of the following actions by the nurse reflects evidence-based practice?
options: Insisting that the client walk now, because the evidence for early walking is strong
Documenting that the client refused, and not bringing up walking again
Asking about the fatigue, explaining the benefits, and agreeing on a time to walk
Reporting the client's noncompliance to the provider right away
questions.rationale:
Asking about the fatigue, explaining the benefits, and agreeing on a time is correct. EBP integrates the evidence with the nurse's expertise and the client's preferences. The nurse respects the client's choice, teaches, and works out a plan the client accepts, then documents it.

Insisting ignores the client's preferences and autonomy. Dropping the subject gives up on teaching and planning. Reporting noncompliance treats a reasonable request as defiance instead of partnering with the client.

Takeaway: The client's preference is one of EBP's three parts: respect it, teach, and plan together.

questions.stem: For each example, specify the concept that it best links to evidence-based practice.
rows: A nurse uses a validated risk tool to choose the best fall-prevention steps for one client.
A nurse's outdated wound care falls below professional standards, and the client sues.
A nurse teaches a client who has heart failure evidence-based ways to limit salt at home.
A unit uses evidence to improve what care it gives, when, and why.
Nurses who base care on evidence can answer for giving clients the best care.
questions.rationale:
Clinical decision making: evidence helps the nurse deliver high-quality care to an individual client. Legal issues: practice that deviates from professional standards creates legal risk. Health, wellness, and illness: evidence guides teaching clients about self-care. Quality improvement: evidence improves the why, when, and what of nursing care. Accountability: EBP lets nurses answer for providing the best care.

Takeaway: EBP touches accountability, decision making, health teaching, legal standards, and quality.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing who defines the standards of nursing care that evidence-based practice helps shape. Which of the following define standards of nursing care?
options: The American Nurses Association (ANA)
The National League for Nursing (NLN)
The Joint Commission
State nurse practice acts
Advertisements from medical supply companies
Individual health care facilities' policies and procedures
questions.rationale:
Standards of nursing care are defined by the ANA, the NLN, The Joint Commission, state nurse practice acts, and individual health care facilities through their policies and procedures. EBP helps define the current best-practice standards.

Supply company advertisements are marketing, not standards, and the companies have a financial interest in what nurses use.

Takeaway: Standards come from professional organizations, accreditors, state law, and your own facility's policies.

questions.stem: For each project, specify whether it is an example of research, evidence-based practice, or quality improvement.
rows: Applying a published guideline on preventing pressure injuries to the unit's care
Testing whether a new music program lowers anxiety, with random assignment and review board approval
Tracking the unit's hand-hygiene rates and changing the process to raise them
Using a systematic review to update the unit's catheter-care procedure
Surveying the unit's clients about wait times to fix the unit's discharge process
questions.rationale:
Research generates new knowledge, usually with a formal design and institutional review board (IRB) approval: testing a music program with random assignment. Evidence-based practice applies existing best evidence to practice: a published guideline, a systematic review. Quality improvement uses a unit's or organization's own data to improve its own processes and outcomes: hand-hygiene rates and discharge wait times.

Takeaway: Research creates evidence, EBP uses evidence, and QI uses local data to improve local processes.

questions.stem: A nurse manager asks staff why they rarely use research in their practice. Which of the following responses describe barriers to evidence-based practice?
options: “I don't have time to look things up during my shift.”
“I'm not sure how to tell whether a study is any good.”
“Our unit has computers with access to nursing databases.”
“We've always done it this way, and it works.”
“My manager gives us paid time for journal club.”
“I don't think research applies to real nursing.”
questions.rationale:
Barriers to EBP include lack of time and heavy workloads, limited knowledge and skill in evaluating evidence, resistance to change from traditional routines, and misperceptions, or not seeing the value of EBP.

Access to nursing databases and paid time for journal club are supports that help overcome barriers, not barriers.

Takeaway: EBP barriers fall into time, skills, access, support, and attitudes, and each has a matching fix.

questions.stem: Staff on a unit say they don't trust “the latest research” and prefer their traditional routine for preventing falls. Which of the following strategies should the nurse manager use first?
options: Order staff to adopt the new practice starting tomorrow
Share the unit's own fall data along with the evidence, and involve staff in planning the change
Wait until every staff member agrees before discussing the evidence
Hire new nurses who already use evidence-based practice
questions.rationale:
Sharing the unit's data with the evidence and involving staff is correct. Resistance to change and not valuing EBP are attitude barriers. Seeing their own unit's outcomes makes the problem real, and involving staff early builds ownership of the change.

Ordering an immediate change usually deepens resistance. Waiting for everyone to agree stalls the change while clients keep falling. Hiring new nurses doesn't address the current staff or the unit's culture.

Takeaway: Overcome resistance with data and involvement, not orders.

questions.stem: A nurse reads research showing that units with more nurses per client have fewer client deaths and complications. Which of the following statements describes how this evidence relates to staffing?
options: It can guide decisions about safe staffing levels, because it links staffing to client outcomes.
It doesn't apply to staffing, because staffing is only a budget decision.
It means every unit must hire more nurses immediately, whatever its clients need.
It applies only to research hospitals, not to community hospitals.
questions.rationale:
It can guide safe staffing decisions is correct. EBP relates to staffing because evidence shows that nurse staffing affects client safety and outcomes, so leaders can use it, together with their own data and their clients' needs, to plan safe staffing.

Only a budget decision ignores the evidence linking staffing to outcomes. Every unit must hire more immediately overstates it: evidence informs decisions alongside each unit's needs. Only research hospitals is wrong: evidence from many settings can apply broadly when it fits the clients.

Takeaway: Evidence about staffing and outcomes is part of how organizations decide what safe staffing is.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements describes the role of accrediting organizations, such as The Joint Commission, in evidence-based practice?
options: They write each hospital's procedures for its nurses to follow.
They conduct most of the nursing research that hospitals use.
They license individual nurses to practice.
They set evidence-based standards that organizations must meet, which pushes facilities to use current evidence.
questions.rationale:
They set evidence-based standards that organizations must meet is correct. Reputable accreditors base their standards on evidence, and organizations must show they meet them, which drives facilities to keep their practice current.

Each hospital writes its own procedures, guided by those standards. Most research is done by researchers at universities, agencies, and health systems, not by accreditors. Licensing nurses is the state board of nursing's job.

Takeaway: Accreditors raise the floor for practice by tying their standards to the evidence.

questions.stem: A unit adopts a structured, evidence-based handoff tool for shift change. Which of the following outcomes is the main reason for this change?
options: Fewer communication errors and gaps in care, which improves client safety
Shorter shifts for the nurses on the unit
Less need to document care in the medical record
Fewer clients admitted to the unit each week
questions.rationale:
Fewer communication errors, which improves safety is correct. EBP relates to communication and safety: evidence shows that structured handoffs keep information from being lost between caregivers, which keeps care continuous across the team.

A handoff tool doesn't shorten shifts, replace documentation, or change admissions.

Takeaway: Evidence-based communication tools make care safer by keeping information intact between caregivers.

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining why evidence-based practice matters for the nursing profession and for clients. Which of the following statements should the nurse include?
options: “It helps ensure the credibility of the nursing profession.”
“It guarantees that every client will recover.”
“It provides accountability for the care nurses give.”
“It means nurses no longer need to follow facility policies.”
“It helps define current best-practice standards of care.”
questions.rationale:
Using EBP helps ensure the credibility of the profession, provides accountability for nursing care, and defines current best-practice standards.

No approach guarantees recovery; evidence improves the odds of good outcomes. EBP doesn't replace facility policies: nurses follow policies as written, and use the facility's process to change them when the evidence supports it.

Takeaway: EBP builds credibility, accountability, and standards, and it works through policy, not around it.

questions.stem: A nurse researcher is planning several studies. Which of the following research questions calls for a qualitative design?
options: Does a daily walking program lower blood pressure more than usual care?
What is it like for family members to care for a parent who has dementia at home?
How many clients on the unit develop pressure injuries each month?
Is there a relationship between hours of sleep and pain scores after surgery?
questions.rationale:
What it's like to care for a parent who has dementia is correct. Qualitative research explores experiences, meanings, and perceptions, using words from interviews, focus groups, and observation.

Does walking lower blood pressure tests an intervention: an experimental, quantitative design. How many clients develop pressure injuries counts: descriptive and quantitative. A relationship between sleep and pain scores uses numbers to find a correlation: quantitative.

Takeaway: “What is it like…?” points to qualitative research; “Does…?”, “How many…?”, and “Is there a relationship…?” point to quantitative research.

questions.stem: For each feature, specify whether it is typical of quantitative or qualitative research.
rows: Data are numbers, such as blood pressure readings and pain scores
Data are words from interviews and observations
The researcher keeps interviewing participants until no new themes appear
A large sample, often randomly selected
Tests a hypothesis about cause and effect
A small sample, chosen on purpose because they have lived the experience
questions.rationale:
Quantitative research uses numbers (measurements, scores, statistics), larger and often random samples, and an objective, controlled approach to test hypotheses and find cause-and-effect relationships.

Qualitative research uses words (interviews, focus groups, observation) and smaller, purposeful samples of people who have lived the experience, and it collects data until no new themes appear, which is called saturation.

Takeaway: Quantitative research counts and tests; qualitative research listens and describes.

questions.stem: A study tests whether a daily walking program lowers blood pressure in older adults. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: In this study, the walking program is the {{0}} variable, and blood pressure is the {{1}} variable.

options: dependent
independent
confounding
control
independent
control
dependent
random

questions.rationale:
The independent variable is what the researcher changes or manipulates, the intervention or “cause”: the walking program. The dependent variable is what's measured, the outcome that depends on it: blood pressure.

A confounding variable is an outside factor that could distort the results. Control describes a comparison group, and random describes how participants are assigned; neither names these variables.

Takeaway: Independent is what I change; dependent is the data I measure.

questions.stem: A nurse is evaluating measurement tools used in research. For each description, specify whether it describes reliability or validity.
rows: Two nurses who use a pain scale on the same client at the same time get the same score.
A questionnaire meant to measure depression really measures depression, not anxiety.
A thermometer gives the same reading three times in a row on the same client.
A fall-risk tool correctly identifies the clients who go on to fall.
questions.rationale:
Reliability is consistency: the tool gives the same results when it's used again, or by different people, under the same conditions, like the pain scale and the thermometer.

Validity is accuracy: the tool measures what it claims to measure, like the depression questionnaire and a fall-risk tool that identifies the clients who fall.

Takeaway: Reliability means repeatable; validity means it truly measures what it should.

questions.stem: In a study of a new mouthwash to prevent mouth sores during chemotherapy, one group of clients uses the mouthwash and another group receives usual mouth care. Which of the following statements describes the purpose of the usual-care group?
options: It gives the researchers a comparison, so they can tell whether the mouthwash made the difference.
It lets the researchers give the mouthwash to more clients.
It makes the study qualitative instead of quantitative.
It protects the clients' confidentiality.
questions.rationale:
It gives a comparison is correct. The control group gets usual care or no intervention. Comparing it with the group that got the intervention shows whether the intervention caused the difference in outcomes.

A control group means fewer clients get the new mouthwash, not more. It doesn't make a study qualitative; controlled comparisons are quantitative. Confidentiality is protected by how data are handled, not by group assignment.

Takeaway: Without a comparison group, you can't tell whether the intervention worked.

questions.stem: Which of the following features makes a study a randomized controlled trial?
options: The researcher interviews participants about their experiences.
The researcher observes and describes a group without changing anything.
Participants are randomly assigned to receive the intervention or usual care.
The researcher compares outcomes before and after a change, without a comparison group.
questions.rationale:
Random assignment to the intervention or usual care is correct. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) has three features: the researcher manipulates an intervention, there's a control group, and participants are randomly assigned, so each has an equal chance of being in either group, which reduces bias.

Interviews about experiences describe qualitative research. Observing without changing anything describes a non-experimental, descriptive design. Before and after without a comparison group is quasi-experimental.

Takeaway: An RCT has an intervention, a control group, and random assignment.

questions.stem: A nurse compares the unit's fall rates for 6 months before and 6 months after starting hourly rounding. There is no comparison unit, and clients weren't randomly assigned. Which of the following designs is this?
options: A randomized controlled trial
A qualitative study
A systematic review
A quasi-experimental study
questions.rationale:
A quasi-experimental study is correct. The nurse made a change (hourly rounding) and measured its effect, but without random assignment or a separate control group, which makes it quasi-experimental.

A randomized controlled trial needs random assignment and a control group. A qualitative study explores experiences in words. A systematic review summarizes many existing studies on one question.

Takeaway: An intervention without randomization or a control group is quasi-experimental, which is weaker evidence than an RCT.

questions.stem: A nurse is searching the literature for evidence. Which of the following are primary sources?
options: A textbook chapter that summarizes many studies on wound care
A journal article written by the researchers who conducted the study
A news story describing a recent study
A thesis in which a nurse researcher reports their own original study
A magazine article in which one author describes another author's work
questions.rationale:
A primary source is the original report of a study by the people who did it: a journal article by the researchers and a thesis reporting the researcher's own study.

A secondary source is one author writing about another author's work: a textbook chapter summarizing studies, a news story about a study, and a magazine article describing another author's work. They're useful for background, but details can be lost or changed in the retelling.

Takeaway: A primary source is the original study by its researchers; a secondary source is someone else's summary.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to understand how clients feel about living with a new ostomy, to improve the unit's teaching. Which of the following types of evidence best answers this question?
options: A randomized controlled trial comparing two brands of ostomy pouches
A cohort study of infection rates after ostomy surgery
Qualitative studies in which clients describe living with an ostomy
An expert's opinion on which ostomy supplies to buy
questions.rationale:
Qualitative studies of clients' experiences is correct. Qualitative studies sit lower on the hierarchy of evidence for whether an intervention works, but they're the best evidence for questions about meaning and experience, which is what this question asks.

A trial of pouch brands and a cohort study of infection rates answer different questions, about effectiveness and risk. Expert opinion is the weakest level of evidence, and it doesn't capture clients' own views.

Takeaway: Match the evidence to the question: for “What is it like?”, qualitative studies are the best evidence.

questions.stem: A nurse is helping recruit clients for a research study on the unit. Which of the following actions protect the participants' rights?
options: Explaining that taking part is voluntary
Telling clients they may leave the study at any time without losing any care
Confirming that an institutional review board (IRB) approved the study
Listing participants' names in the unit newsletter to thank them
Promising participants that the new treatment will work
Keeping each participant's data confidential
questions.rationale:
Research ethics protect participants through voluntary participation, the right to withdraw at any time without penalty, approval by an institutional review board (IRB), and confidentiality of their data. These rest on respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.

Publishing participants' names breaks confidentiality. Promising that a treatment will work is dishonest and undermines informed consent; the study exists because the answer isn't known yet.

Takeaway: Participants must be informed, take part voluntarily, be free to withdraw, be in an IRB-approved study, and have their data kept confidential.

questions.stem: A nurse is appraising a study showing that a new wound dressing heals wounds faster. The company that makes the dressing paid for the study, and its own employees analyzed the data. Which of the following conclusions should the nurse draw?
options: The results must be accurate, since the company knows its product best.
The study should be ignored completely, because companies can't do research.
The funding source doesn't matter once a study is published.
The possible conflict of interest calls for caution and a search for independent studies.
questions.rationale:
Caution and a search for independent studies is correct. Appraising evidence includes judging its credibility, and a sponsor that analyzes data about its own product has a conflict of interest that could bias the results. Independent studies that find the same thing would make the evidence more trustworthy.

Accepting the results because the company knows the product ignores the bias. Ignoring the study completely overcorrects: industry-funded studies can be valid, but they need scrutiny. Publication alone doesn't remove bias.

Takeaway: When appraising a study, ask who paid for it and who analyzed the data.

questions.stem: A nurse researcher is planning a study. Place the steps of the research process in order.
items: Identify the problem or research question
Review the literature
Write the hypothesis and define the variables
Choose the design, sample, and methods
Collect and analyze the data
Interpret and share the findings
questions.rationale:
The research process moves from identifying the problem, to reviewing the literature to learn what's already known, to writing a hypothesis and defining the variables, to choosing the design, sample, and methods, to collecting and analyzing data, and finally to interpreting and sharing (disseminating) the findings so others can use them.

Takeaway: Know the question and the literature before planning the study, and share the results at the end so they can become evidence.

questions.stem: A nurse is choosing articles to support a practice change. Which of the following features increases confidence in an article's quality?
options: It was reviewed by experts in the field before it was published.
It was shared widely on social media.
It was written in plain, easy-to-read language.
It was published on the website of a company that sells the product.
questions.rationale:
Reviewed by experts before publication is correct. In peer review, experts evaluate an article's methods and conclusions before a journal publishes it, which helps screen out weak or biased work. Every source should still be judged for credibility.

Social media shares measure popularity, not quality. Plain language helps readers but says nothing about the quality of the study. A company that sells the product has a conflict of interest.

Takeaway: Look for peer-reviewed sources, and judge every source for credibility.

questions.stem: A nurse writes this question: “In adults who have type 2 diabetes, does a text-message reminder program, compared with printed instructions, improve medication adherence over 3 months?” Which part of the question is the outcome (O)?
options: Adults who have type 2 diabetes
Improved medication adherence
Printed instructions
Over 3 months
questions.rationale:
Improved medication adherence is correct. The outcome is the result being measured. In this PICOT question, P = adults who have type 2 diabetes, I = a text-message reminder program, C = printed instructions, O = medication adherence, and T = over 3 months.

Adults who have type 2 diabetes is the population, printed instructions is the comparison (the alternative to the intervention), and over 3 months is the time.

Takeaway: The outcome is what you measure; the comparison is the alternative to the intervention.

questions.stem: A nurse is leading an evidence-based practice project to improve pain control after knee replacement. For each activity, specify the step of the evidence-based practice process.
rows: Searches CINAHL and MEDLINE for studies on cold therapy after knee surgery
Notices that clients' pain scores after knee replacement are higher than the hospital's goal
Compares pain scores for 3 months after the change with the scores from before
Writes a focused question in PICOT format
Starts the new cold-therapy routine, combining the evidence with clients' preferences
Judges each study's quality and whether its participants resemble the unit's clients
questions.rationale:
The EBP process starts with the client: Assess (notice the clinical problem: high pain scores), Ask (write a focused PICOT question), Acquire (search credible databases such as CINAHL and MEDLINE), Appraise (judge quality, validity, and fit with the unit's clients), Apply (put the evidence into practice with clinical expertise and client preferences), and Evaluate (compare outcomes after the change with the baseline).

Takeaway: Assess, Ask, Acquire, Appraise, Apply, Evaluate. The textbook's four steps (ask, retrieve, appraise, apply and evaluate) follow the same order.

questions.stem: A nurse is looking for credible evidence about preventing falls in older adults. Which of the following sources should the nurse use?
options: The CINAHL database of nursing and health literature
A personal blog about home remedies
The Cochrane Library of systematic reviews
A video posted by a celebrity on social media
A clinical practice guideline from a professional organization
questions.rationale:
Credible sources include databases such as CINAHL (and MEDLINE or PubMed), the Cochrane Library of systematic reviews, and clinical practice guidelines from professional organizations and agencies. Nursing databases may give abstracts or full text, and many offer tutorials.

A personal blog and a celebrity's video aren't peer-reviewed and often aren't based on research. Every source should be judged for credibility.

Takeaway: Acquire evidence from peer-reviewed databases, systematic reviews, and professional guidelines.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing journal articles for an evidence-based practice project. Which of the following should the nurse look for in each article?
options: An overview of the study, including how it was done
The number of times the article was shared online
A conclusion based on the study's results
Relevant references to other research
Whether the author's opinion matches the nurse's own
questions.rationale:
In a literature review, nurses look for the article's scientific elements: an overview of the study, including its methodology, a written conclusion based on the study's results, and relevant references. These show whether the study can be judged and trusted.

Online shares measure popularity, not quality. Agreeing with the nurse's opinion isn't a standard of evidence; looking only for agreement is bias.

Takeaway: Judge an article by its methods, its results-based conclusion, and its references, not by its popularity or whether you agree with it.

questions.stem: A unit has started a new evidence-based routine. Before judging the results, the team checks whether nurses on every shift are carrying out the routine the way it was designed. Which of the following statements explains why?
options: Checking how the routine is carried out replaces the need to measure client outcomes.
If the routine isn't carried out as intended, the results can't show whether the routine itself works.
Nurses who don't follow the routine exactly must be disciplined.
The routine can be changed only if every nurse agrees to it.
questions.rationale:
If the routine isn't carried out as intended, the results can't show whether it works is correct. Evaluating a practice change begins at implementation: the team monitors that the change is carried out as intended, then analyzes the outcome data. Poor results from a routine that wasn't followed say nothing about the routine itself.

Monitoring the process doesn't replace measuring outcomes; both are needed. The purpose is improvement, not discipline. A change doesn't need every nurse's agreement; it goes through the organization's process.

Takeaway: Check that a change was actually carried out as designed before you judge whether it worked.

questions.stem: A unit tried a new routine for reassessing pain 1 hour after pain medication. After 3 months, clients' satisfaction with pain control rose on the day shift, but night-shift nurses often missed the reassessments. Which of the following actions should the team take?
options: Reject the routine, since it didn't work on every shift
Accept the routine unchanged and spread it to every unit
Modify the routine for the night shift and keep monitoring the results
Stop collecting data, since satisfaction already improved
questions.rationale:
Modify the routine for nights and keep monitoring is correct. After evaluating a change, the team can accept, reject, or modify it. The routine helped when it was carried out, so the problem is how it fits the night shift, which calls for changing the process and then monitoring again.

Rejecting it throws away a practice that worked. Spreading it unchanged carries the night-shift problem to every unit. Stopping data collection ends evaluation before the problem is fixed.

Takeaway: Evaluation leads to accepting, rejecting, or modifying the change, and then the cycle continues.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to find evidence on reducing anxiety in children having blood drawn. Which of the following questions is written in a focused, searchable PICOT format?
options: “What do pediatric nurses believe is the best way to calm children during blood draws?”
“In school-age children having blood drawn, does a distraction toy, compared with no distraction, lower anxiety scores during the procedure?”
“Is a distraction toy a good idea, and should every hospital buy them for children?”
“How do children of all ages feel about needles and medical procedures in general?”
questions.rationale:
The question with all five parts is correct: P = school-age children having blood drawn, I = a distraction toy, C = no distraction, O = anxiety scores, T = during the procedure. A focused PICOT question is specific and searchable.

What nurses believe asks for opinion, not evidence about an intervention. Is it a good idea, and should every hospital buy them is vague and asks two questions at once. How children feel about needles in general is too broad to search well.

Takeaway: A good clinical question names the population, intervention, comparison, outcome, and time.

questions.stem: A 3-month pilot of a new oral-care routine lowered pneumonia rates on one unit, with no new problems found. Which of the following steps should come next to make the routine part of everyday care?
options: Ask each nurse to decide whether to use the routine
Work with management to revise the facility's policy and procedure to include the routine
End the routine, since the pilot is over
Keep the routine on the pilot unit only, without telling other units
questions.rationale:
Revising the facility's policy and procedure with management is correct. If a change is beneficial, the team works with management to update the facility's policies and procedures, so the change becomes part of the nursing routine.

Leaving it to each nurse makes care inconsistent. Ending it throws away a change that worked. Keeping it on one unit in silence withholds a benefit from other clients; successful methods should be shared.

Takeaway: A successful pilot becomes routine through the facility's policies and procedures.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of individual evidence-based practice?
options: A hospital's practice council updates the policy on preventing falls.
A health system adopts a new sepsis screening protocol in every emergency department.
A nurse uses a current guideline to teach assigned clients heart failure self-care, within unit policy.
Nursing leadership funds a new evidence-based practice fellowship.
questions.rationale:
A nurse using a current guideline with assigned clients, within policy is correct. Individual EBP is a single nurse at the point of care: asking questions about their own practice, reading, and applying evidence to their own clients within current policy.

A council updating policy, a system-wide protocol, and leadership funding a fellowship are organizational EBP: changes and resources at the level of the unit, facility, or system.

Takeaway: Individual EBP is one nurse, their own clients, within policy; organizational EBP is system-wide change.

questions.stem: A hospital wants to build evidence-based practice across the organization. Which of the following should it put in place?
options: Leadership support and a culture that encourages questions
Funding and protected time for EBP projects
A rule that each nurse changes procedures alone whenever they find a new study
An EBP council that includes nurse researchers and librarians
Access to databases and references at the point of care
questions.rationale:
Organizational EBP needs leadership support and a culture of inquiry, resources such as funding and protected time, people with expertise such as an EBP council, nurse researchers, librarians, and mentors, and access to evidence where care happens. These turn evidence into standardized, lasting change.

Each nurse changing procedures alone creates inconsistent care and bypasses policy; changes go through the organization's process.

Takeaway: Organizations sustain EBP with leadership, resources, expert support, and access to evidence.

questions.stem: A hospital's evidence-based practice council uses the Iowa Model to guide its practice changes. Which of the following statements describes the purpose of a formal EBP model like this one?
options: It replaces the need for nurses to read research.
It lets each nurse change unit procedures independently.
It is a law that every hospital must follow.
It gives a step-by-step structure for making practice changes across the organization.
questions.rationale:
A step-by-step structure for organization-wide change is correct. Formal EBP models, such as the Iowa Model, the Johns Hopkins model, ACE Star, and Stetler, guide an organization through identifying a problem, finding and appraising evidence, piloting a change, and spreading it through policies and protocols.

A model doesn't replace reading research; it organizes how evidence is used. It doesn't let individual nurses change procedures independently; changes go through the organization's process. It's a framework, not a law.

Takeaway: A formal EBP model is the organization's roadmap for evidence-based change.

questions.stem: A nurse is comparing individual and organizational evidence-based practice. Which of the following statements is accurate?
options: Individual EBP is quicker and specific to one client; organizational EBP takes longer but standardizes care and has a larger, lasting impact.
Individual EBP changes the facility's policy manual, while organizational EBP affects the care of only one client at a time.
Individual EBP depends on leadership support and funding, while organizational EBP needs only one interested nurse.
Individual and organizational EBP are the same process and differ only in which department pays for the work.
questions.rationale:
Individual EBP is quicker and client-specific; organizational EBP takes longer but standardizes care with a larger, lasting impact is correct. Individual EBP is one nurse applying evidence to their own clients within current policy. Organizational EBP involves leaders, councils, and committees changing policies and protocols across a unit or system, and it lasts.

The second and third options swap the two levels: organizational EBP changes the policy manual and needs leadership support, funding, and resources. Only who pays ignores the real differences in scope and process.

Takeaway: Individual EBP is fast and personal; organizational EBP is slower, standardized, and bigger.

questions.stem: A staff nurse wants to encourage coworkers to use evidence in their practice. Which of the following actions is the most effective?
options: Telling coworkers they're wrong whenever they follow routine practices
Waiting for the nurse manager to bring up evidence-based practice
Starting a monthly unit journal club that discusses a current article
Changing the unit's shared procedures on their own when they find a new study
questions.rationale:
A monthly journal club is correct. Journal clubs build skill in reading and appraising research, make evidence part of the unit's culture, and help overcome attitude barriers such as misperceptions and low confidence.

Criticizing coworkers creates resistance. Waiting for the manager leaves the theory-practice gap open. Changing shared procedures alone bypasses policy; changes go through the facility's process.

Takeaway: Staff nurses spread EBP by building skills and culture, like journal clubs, not by going around policy.

questions.stem: A hospital plans to introduce an evidence-based routine for giving handoff report at the bedside. Why should it pilot the routine on one or two units before using it everywhere?
options: To avoid having to measure any results
Because evidence-based changes are never used hospital-wide
So the units that don't take part can keep their own procedures permanently
To test the change on a small scale, find problems, and measure results before spreading it
questions.rationale:
Testing small, finding problems, and measuring results before spreading is correct. Pilot testing is part of organizational EBP: it shows whether the change works in this setting and lets the team fix problems before a facility-wide rollout.

A pilot exists to measure results, not to avoid measuring them. Successful changes are spread hospital-wide, through policy. Other units don't keep their own procedures permanently; once the change proves itself, it becomes the standard.

Takeaway: Pilot it small, measure it, fix it, then spread it.

questions.stem: Which of the following recognitions requires a hospital to show that evidence-based practice is built into the organization?
options: Healthy People 2030
A state nursing license
Medicare Part A eligibility
Magnet recognition from the American Nurses Credentialing Center
questions.rationale:
Magnet recognition is correct. The American Nurses Credentialing Center's Magnet program recognizes nursing excellence, and it requires the organization to show that evidence-based practice and research are part of its nursing practice. Organizational EBP supports Magnet status.

Healthy People 2030 sets national health objectives. A state nursing license lets an individual practice. Medicare Part A is hospital insurance coverage for clients.

Takeaway: Magnet status signals a hospital culture of nursing excellence, including evidence-based practice.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings from the unit observations that suggest a practice problem the nurse should address.
questions.passage:
[[28% of clients 70 and older developed delirium, compared with 15% on similar units]].
[[Overhead lights are turned on for vital signs at 0000 and 0400 for every client]].
[[Glasses and hearing aids are usually kept in bedside drawers]].
[[Sleeping pills are given on request]].
[[Families are encouraged to visit]].
[[A large clock and calendar hang in each room]].
questions.rationale:
The cues of a practice problem are a delirium rate nearly double that of similar units, lights on for every client at 0000 and 0400 (broken sleep), glasses and hearing aids left in drawers (sensory deprivation, which raises confusion), and sleeping pills on request (sedating medications raise the risk of delirium in older adults).

Family visits and a clock and calendar help orient clients; they're strengths to keep.

Takeaway: EBP starts with assessing: compare your data with a benchmark, and look at current routines for the cause.

questions.stem: The nurse writes a PICOT question to guide the search. Complete the question.
questions.text: In {{0}}, does {{1}}, compared with {{2}}, reduce {{3}} during the hospital stay?

options: nurses on the medical unit
hospitalized adults 70 and older
all adults in the community
family members of older adults
a routine of reorientation, sleep, walking, and sensory aids, without medication
a sleeping pill for every client at bedtime
more vital-sign checks at night
a larger calendar in each room
no hospital stay
a sleeping pill on request
usual care
family visits
the unit's costs
nurses' overtime
the number of visitors
new cases of delirium

questions.rationale:
A useful PICOT question for this problem: P = hospitalized adults 70 and older; I = a routine of reorientation, sleep, walking, and sensory aids, without medication; C = usual care; O = new cases of delirium; T = during the hospital stay.

Nurses and family members aren't the clients at risk, and all adults in the community is the wrong population. Sleeping pills and more night checks add risk instead of testing a solution, and a bigger calendar is too small to be the intervention. Usual care is the natural comparison. Costs, overtime, and visitors aren't the client outcome the nurse is worried about.

Takeaway: Build the PICOT question from the assessed problem: the clients at risk, the intervention, usual care, and the outcome you want to change.

questions.stem: Place the four sources the nurse found in order, from the strongest to the weakest evidence about whether a program reduces delirium.
items: The systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 randomized controlled trials
The single randomized controlled trial at one hospital
The qualitative study of family members' experiences
The opinion article by a hospital executive
questions.rationale:
In the hierarchy of evidence for whether an intervention works, a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials is strongest (Level I), a single well-designed RCT is next (Level II), a single qualitative study is lower (Level VI), and expert opinion is weakest (Level VII).

The qualitative study is still valuable: it's the best evidence about what families experience, just not about whether the program works.

Takeaway: For “Does it work?”, a meta-analysis of RCTs is strongest and opinion is weakest.

questions.stem: Until the hospital's policy changes, the nurse wants to use the evidence with assigned clients. For each potential action, specify whether it is indicated or not indicated.
rows: Make sure clients wear their glasses and hearing aids during the day
Skip the 0000 and 0400 vital signs for clients who seem stable
Dim the lights and keep noise down at night, while still doing the required checks
Help clients walk in the hall during the day, as their condition allows
Give every older adult a sleeping pill on admission, as the opinion article suggests
Present the evidence to the unit's practice council and propose a change to the night vital-signs policy
questions.rationale:
Individual EBP works within current policy. The nurse can keep glasses and hearing aids in use, dim the lights and reduce noise while still doing the required checks, and help clients walk: each is supported by the evidence and allowed by policy. To change the policy itself, the nurse brings the evidence to the practice council, which is the organization's process.

Skipping required vital signs violates the policy as written, even with good evidence. A sleeping pill for every older adult follows the weakest source and contradicts the stronger evidence: sedating medications raise the risk of delirium.

Takeaway: Use the evidence where policy allows, and change the policy through the organization's process.

questions.stem: Six months after the hospital adopts the new routine, the council reviews the unit's results. For each finding, specify whether it shows improvement, no change, or a decline.
rows: New delirium in clients 70 and older: 28% → 16%
Average length of stay: 5.1 → 5.1 days
Night-shift staff trained in the routine: 95% → 70%, after many new hires
